title: Louis de Montfort (1673–1716)
hookLine: to Jesus through Mary: a total consecration

cards: Villagers are carrying earth in baskets up a hill in Brittany. A poor priest in a worn cassock has talked them into building a calvary: a mound, a path, a cross on top, so people can walk and pray the Passion.
They dig, haul and build. Tradition says that on the eve of the blessing, an order arrives: tear it down. The authorities fear it could be used as a fort.
Tradition says the priest took the news quietly and said, blessed be God. His name is Louis-Marie Grignion de Montfort, and he is remembered for one phrase in particular.

teach.b: First, the preacher. Louis de Montfort spent his life on the road in western France, preaching missions in villages, teaching the rosary, and writing hymns people could sing to tunes they already knew.
Some bishops welcomed him; others sent him away. He founded communities that carried on after him, among them the Daughters of Wisdom.
Second, the phrase: to Jesus through Mary. In his book True Devotion to Mary, the goal is Jesus. Mary is the way he chose because, he wrote, she is the surest and gentlest road to her Son.
Every true devotion to her, he says, ends in him.

Montfort proposed a consecration: after a time of preparation, a person gives everything to Jesus through Mary's hands, body, soul, possessions, even the good of one's prayers and good deeds, holding nothing back.
Catholics still make it, often on a feast of Mary. Pope John Paul II took his motto, Totus tuus, all yours, from this tradition. Fourth, what Mary herself says.

teach.h: WHATSOEVER HE SHALL SAY TO YOU.
teach.b: At the wedding at Cana, in John's Gospel, she tells the servants, in the Douay-Rheims: "Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye." She points away from herself.

At the cross, Jesus says to the beloved disciple, "Behold thy mother," and the disciple takes her as his own. Catholic tradition reads that as a gift to every disciple. Worship belongs to God alone, the Church teaches.
Mary, in Montfort's picture, is the mother who walks you to her Son.

how: Catholics who make Montfort's consecration usually follow a period of prayer and reading from his True Devotion to Mary, then consecrate themselves on a Marian feast, and some renew it each year.

o: Latin for God alone, a hermit's motto
Latin for all yours, a gift of oneself
Latin for all together, a call to unity

games.q: Louis de Montfort — tap the pairs.

s: it ends with Jesus. to Jesus through Mary: every true devotion to her, he says, ends in him.
the Church teaches that worship belongs to God alone
Mary is honored as the mother of Jesus, not worshiped.
at Cana, Mary tells the servants to do whatever Jesus says
"Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye." she points away from herself.

games.q: you're Montfort. the villagers have built the calvary with you, basket by basket. on the eve of the blessing, an order comes to tear it down. what do you do?
o: refuse, and stand guard on the hill.
accept it quietly and bless God anyway.
games.why: tradition says he took it calmly and said, blessed be God, then went on preaching.

practice: Walk through the rest of today in your mind, hour by hour: the work, the meals, the people, the dull stretches. If you pray, say the Hail Mary slowly and hand each piece of the day to her, to carry to her Son.
If you don't, choose one person who has mothered you and offer the day in their honor, doing each task the way they'd hope to see it done.

wordCard.voice: Totus tuus. Latin for all yours, the total consecration to Jesus through Mary that Louis de Montfort taught, and the motto Pope John Paul II took from him.

orig.note: Latin: all yours, the heart of Montfort's consecration and Pope John Paul II's motto.

carryVoice: Your line: to Jesus through Mary. At Cana, she pointed away from herself and toward him. Until tomorrow.
